Where this week's projections come from

Each player's number blends, where he has one from each:

  • our model and ESPN's projection, 48% and 52%, measured on 1789 graded games;
  • the betting market's implied points, 33% where books priced him (less when only one or two did; 11 of your 14 players this week), measured on 882 graded games;
  • the FantasyPros consensus projection, 22% (11 of your 14 players), measured on 1415 graded games.

Each weight is the one that would have been most accurate on this season's finished games, pulled toward its starting value until enough are graded. Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

Most valuable players

Value is points above a waiver pickup at his position, summed over weeks 9-17: what he is simulated to score each week he plays, less what the pickup would. Weeks he misses (byes, injuries, a reported timeline) count nothing, so a hurt star drops down. Upside is that value in his best tenth of simulated seasons: a breakout, a bigger role, a clean bill of health. Pickup level a game: QB 14.5, RB 7.7, WR 9.4, TE 8.6, K 10.4, D/ST 10.1. RoS/g is his season value a game and Δwk its move since last week (green up, red down, yellow flat; deeper is bigger -- tap Δwk for the risers, again for the fallers), Wk this week's projection, G games expected, Range his points a week (10th-90th percentile) and Mkt what the rest of the league sees him worth a game (those three on wider screens). Tap a column to sort; your players are highlighted. Tap a player's name for his game log: points, snap share and stat line, week by week.

Best D/ST and K for this matchup

Free agents and your own, each swapped into your recommended lineup and scored against your opponent on the same correlated simulations. A defence facing your own quarterback hedges him: that steadies your score, which helps when you are favoured and hurts when you are not. Gaps under half a point are noise. Range is the 15th to 85th percentile of the unit's simulated score: a defence's floor is often a point or two, so a high ceiling with a low floor is a boom-or-bust pick.

Betting

Prop lines that look wrong. For each player and stat, the other books' quotes (their margin taken out; Pinnacle, the sharpest, counts double) are fitted to one curve of his outcomes, so any line can be priced: a book at 30.5 rushing yards when the rest sit near 72 shows as a near-certain over. Ours is the chance from our own projection of that stat and how much such projections miss by (2021-2025). Combined leans toward the books on yards (they know the matchup) and toward ours where we have been as good. EV is the expected profit per unit staked at that price: on the books' chance, and on the combined one. Way off: 10%+ on both the books' read and ours. One-sided markets (anytime touchdown) are left out.

Prices pulled with the last refresh (Sun 10:23 AM ET); props move fast, so check the book before betting. Books limit accounts that keep taking prices well off the market.

Parlays

Two or three of the recommended bets above, at the same book and from different games (so they don't move together). A parlay pays the legs' odds multiplied and wins only if all do, so a parlay of good prices multiplies the edge — and the error in the chances, and the book's margin on any leg that isn't an edge. It wins far less often, so keep the stake smaller than a single bet's. Legs avg is what the same legs earn as separate bets.

Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Tap a column heading to sort.

Betting

Prop lines that look wrong. For each player and stat, the other books' quotes (their margin taken out; Pinnacle, the sharpest, counts double) are fitted to one curve of his outcomes, so any line can be priced: a book at 30.5 rushing yards when the rest sit near 72 shows as a near-certain over. Ours is the chance from our own projection of that stat and how much such projections miss by (2021-2025). Combined leans toward the books on yards (they know the matchup) and toward ours where we have been as good. EV is the expected profit per unit staked at that price: on the books' chance, and on the combined one. Way off: 10%+ on both the books' read and ours. One-sided markets (anytime touchdown) are left out.

Prices pulled with the last refresh (Sun 10:23 AM ET); props move fast, so check the book before betting. Books limit accounts that keep taking prices well off the market.

Parlays

Two or three of the recommended bets above, at the same book and from different games (so they don't move together). A parlay pays the legs' odds multiplied and wins only if all do, so a parlay of good prices multiplies the edge — and the error in the chances, and the book's margin on any leg that isn't an edge. It wins far less often, so keep the stake smaller than a single bet's. Legs avg is what the same legs earn as separate bets.

Game lines: spreads, moneylines, totals

The same check on the main markets. Each book's price against the other books' read; a spread or total at a different number is priced on how often NFL games end on each margin and total (since 1999) -- half a point around 3 or 7 is worth far more than elsewhere. Wins is the chance the bet wins at that number (a push returns the stake). No opinion of ours on who wins: main lines are the sharpest market there is, so expect few.

Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Tap a column heading to sort.
